lead: Take a square matrix A. Its characteristic polynomial p(λ) = det(λI − A) is built from A, so A can be fed back into it: replace λ by A, and replace the constant term by a multiple of the identity. Cayley-Hamilton says the result is always the zero matrix. This free identity turns high powers of A into low powers, gives a formula for A⁻¹ when det A ≠ 0, and leads to the minimal polynomial, the smallest polynomial that kills A. Exams ask for verification on 2×2 and 3×3 matrices and for these two uses.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for det(A − λI) and eigenvalues, and Unit 1 for matrix multiplication and inverses.

blocks.text: The characteristic polynomial of an n×n matrix A is p(λ) = det(λI − A). Expanding the determinant gives a monic polynomial of degree n.

blocks.where: p(λ) is the characteristic polynomial of A; the c<sub>k</sub> are its coefficients; c<sub>0</sub> = p(0) = det(−A) = (−1)<sup>n</sup> det A; c<sub>n−1</sub> = −trace(A).

blocks.text: Some books write det(A − λI). That is (−1)<sup>n</sup>p(λ), and it also vanishes at A, so the theorem below is unchanged.

blocks.where: A is the n×n matrix; I is the n×n identity; 0 is the n×n zero matrix. This is the Cayley-Hamilton theorem: every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial.

blocks.text: The right side is a matrix. Powers of A are matrix products, and c<sub>0</sub>I means the scalar c<sub>0</sub> on the diagonal. The theorem is surprising because A has infinitely many powers, yet one relation of degree n controls all of them: A<sup>n</sup> is a combination of I, A, …, A<sup>n−1</sup>, and multiplying by A reduces every higher power the same way.
For n = 2, p(λ) = λ² − (tr A)λ + det A, so A² − (tr A)A + (det A)I = 0. Write A = [[a, b], [c, d]] and expand: every entry cancels. That is the whole 2×2 verification.

sections.h3: Reducing powers and finding the inverse

blocks.text: Two exam uses follow from one rearrangement. Solve p(A) = 0 for the highest power.

blocks.where: the symbols are as above; the right side uses only powers below n.

blocks.text: For a 2×2 matrix, A² = (tr A)A − (det A)I. Multiply by A to get A³ = (tr A)A² − (det A)A, then replace A² again. Every power ends as αA + βI.
For the inverse, suppose c<sub>0</sub> ≠ 0. With p(λ) = det(λI − A), c<sub>0</sub> = (−1)<sup>n</sup> det A, so this is det A ≠ 0. Move c<sub>0</sub>I across and factor out A.

blocks.where: the bracket is an n×n matrix; −c<sub>0</sub>I is a nonzero multiple of the identity, so A is invertible.

blocks.text: Multiply by A⁻¹ and divide by −c<sub>0</sub>. For n = 2, c<sub>1</sub> = −tr A and c<sub>0</sub> = det A, giving the formula below.
A⁻¹ = (1/det A)((tr A)I − A), det A ≠ 0
blocks.where: tr A is the sum of the diagonal entries; det A is the determinant; I is the 2×2 identity. The order matters: it is (tr A)I − A, not A − (tr A)I.

blocks.text: These formulas beat Gauss-Jordan for small matrices with simple entries, and they are expected when a question says 'hence find A⁻¹' after a Cayley-Hamilton check.

An annihilating polynomial of A is any nonzero polynomial q(λ) with q(A) = 0. The characteristic polynomial is one, by Cayley-Hamilton. Among all annihilating polynomials, choose one of least degree and make its leading coefficient 1. That is the minimal polynomial m(λ). It is unique.

items: m divides every annihilating polynomial, so m divides p.
m and p have the same roots, namely the eigenvalues of A. Only multiplicities can differ.
deg m ≤ n, and m = p exactly when every eigenvalue has the same multiplicity in m as in p, that is, when the largest Jordan block for each eigenvalue is as large as its algebraic multiplicity.

blocks.text: Diagonalization criterion: A is diagonalizable over F if and only if m(λ) splits into distinct linear factors over F, that is m(λ) = (λ − λ1)(λ − λ2)⋯(λ − λk) with distinct λi. The full test comes in 4.4; the minimal polynomial gives the quickest version.
When m is smaller than p, and when it is not:

items: A = diag(2, 2, 3): p(λ) = (λ − 2)²(λ − 3), and (A − 2I)(A − 3I) = 0, so m(λ) = (λ − 2)(λ − 3). The degree drops because eigenvalue 2 has two independent eigenvectors.

And when it is not: A = [[2, 1], [0, 2]] has p(λ) = (λ − 2)², A − 2I = [[0, 1], [0, 0]] ≠ 0, and (A − 2I)² = 0, so m(λ) = (λ − 2)². Here m = p. A repeated eigenvalue alone does not lower the degree; too few eigenvectors does.

blocks.text: Reading m from data: distinct eigenvalues force m = p. With repeated eigenvalues, test (A − λI), (A − λI)², … and multiply over the distinct eigenvalues until the product kills A.

figure.caption: The characteristic polynomial is the handle: Cayley-Hamilton sets p(A) to the zero matrix, which gives power reduction and the inverse. The minimal polynomial is the lowest-degree polynomial that does the same job.

spec.title: Polynomial handle
spec.aria: Cayley-Hamilton connects a matrix to its characteristic polynomial and supports power reduction, inverse computation, and the minimal polynomial.

examples.question: For A = [[1, 2], [0, 3]]: (a) verify the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, (b) use it to find A⁻¹, (c) state the minimal polynomial.
steps: Characteristic polynomial: λI − A = [[λ − 1, −2], [0, λ − 3]], so p(λ) = (λ − 1)(λ − 3) = λ² − 4λ + 3. Check: trace = 1 + 3 = 4, determinant = 3.
Inverse: multiply p(A) = 0 by A⁻¹: A − 4I + 3A⁻¹ = 0.
Minimal polynomial: eigenvalues 1 and 3 are distinct. Any annihilator vanishes at both, so m(λ) = (λ − 1)(λ − 3) = λ² − 4λ + 3 = p(λ).
examples.answer: p(A) = 0 for A = [[1, 2], [0, 3]], A⁻¹ = [[1, −2/3], [0, 1/3]], and the minimal polynomial is λ² − 4λ + 3, equal to the characteristic polynomial.

traps: p(A) = 0 means the zero matrix. Writing p(λ) = 0 for every scalar λ is false; p has only the n eigenvalues as roots.
The minimal polynomial divides p but can be a proper factor. Check 2I or diag(2, 2, 3) before assuming m = p.
A repeated eigenvalue does not by itself make m smaller than p. The block [[2, 1], [0, 2]] has m = p = (λ − 2)².
In A⁻¹ = (1/det A)((tr A)I − A), reversing the order gives −A⁻¹. Signs are the commonest lost marks.

For n = 3, det(A − λI) = −p(λ). That polynomial also kills A, because −p(A) = 0. But it is not monic, its constant term is det A rather than (−1)³det A, and its λ² coefficient is +tr A rather than −tr A. Feeding these into the inverse formula flips signs. So expand det(λI − A), or multiply det(A − λI) by (−1)³ before reading coefficients.

quiz.q: State the Cayley-Hamilton theorem for an n×n matrix A.
quiz.a: With p(λ) = det(λI − A) = λⁿ + c<sub>n−1</sub>λ<sup>n−1</sup> + ⋯ + c<sub>0</sub>, we get Aⁿ + c<sub>n−1</sub>A<sup>n−1</sup> + ⋯ + c<sub>0</sub>I = 0, the n×n zero matrix.

quiz.q: Define the minimal polynomial of A.
quiz.a: The monic polynomial of least degree among all nonzero polynomials q with q(A) = 0.

quiz.q: For a 2×2 matrix, why does p(A) = 0 let you write A³ using only A and I?
quiz.a: p(A) = 0 gives A² = (tr A)A − (det A)I. Multiply by A: A³ = (tr A)A² − (det A)A, then substitute the expression for A². The result is a combination of A and I.

quiz.q: The minimal polynomial divides the characteristic polynomial and has the same roots. What does this say about eigenvalues and multiplicities?
quiz.a: Both polynomials have exactly the eigenvalues as roots, so no eigenvalue is added or lost. Only the multiplicities can be smaller in m.

quiz.q: For the same A, use Cayley-Hamilton to find A⁻¹.
Find the minimal polynomial of A = diag(2, 2, 3).
quiz.a: (A − 2I)(A − 3I) = 0 and neither factor alone kills A, so m(λ) = (λ − 2)(λ − 3).

quiz.q: A 3×3 matrix has characteristic polynomial (λ − 2)²(λ − 5). List the possible minimal polynomials and say which make A diagonalizable.
quiz.a: The minimal polynomial must have roots 2 and 5. Possible choices: (λ − 2)(λ − 5), which splits into distinct linear factors, so A is diagonalizable; or (λ − 2)²(λ − 5), which has a repeated factor, so A is not diagonalizable. A polynomial missing 2 or 5 is impossible because every eigenvalue must be a root.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same identity powers matrix functions: e<sup>At</sup> is computed by reducing its series with p(A) = 0, a standard step in control theory and circuit analysis. Numerical software avoids exact high powers and uses Krylov subspaces instead, but the minimal polynomial still measures how soon the sequence I, A, A², … becomes linearly dependent. Search 'matrix function', 'Jordan form', 'rational canonical form' and 'Krylov method' to continue.
